messages.content: I want to design an ownership type checker for cancellable asynchronous tasks that can safely transfer borrowed resources across task boundaries. It needs to guarantee memory safety under cancellation and task migration, without whole-program analysis or runtime borrow checks. It should also accept 12 safe programs and reject 12 unsafe programs covering nested borrows, ownership transfer, and cancellation.

The central question is whether a task can still access a borrowed resource after the resource has ceased to be valid. The checker’s design needs to rule that out even when a task is cancelled or migrates. Those are requirements on the safety guarantee, not merely cases to handle when execution proceeds normally. The requested evaluation is specific: accept 12 safe programs and reject 12 unsafe programs, with the programs covering nested borrows, ownership transfer, and cancellation.
What does transferring a borrowed resource across a task boundary mean in this context?

Conceptually, a task receives access to a resource it does not necessarily own. Crossing the boundary matters because the borrower’s ability to access the resource may now persist independently of the code that supplied the borrow. For that access to be memory-safe, the resource must remain valid for every point at which the receiving task can use it. The goal does not specify a particular language construct or representation for making the transfer.
So moving a borrow into a task is not the same as transferring ownership of the resource?

Right. Borrowing concerns temporary access; ownership concerns who is responsible for the resource and can ultimately relinquish it. A checker must keep those questions distinct when reasoning about a task boundary. A task receiving borrowed access cannot safely use that access after the resource’s validity ends, regardless of whether the owner is another task or some surrounding computation. Ownership transfer is also within the requested program coverage, but the goal does not prescribe its exact syntax or rules.
Why does cancellation make the borrowing question harder?

Because the checker cannot rely solely on the path where a task finishes normally. Cancellation can change when task activity stops and when access to a resource ends. The safety condition still has to hold: cancellation must not leave a task able to use a borrow after its resource becomes invalid. That statement describes what must be proved, not a particular cancellation mechanism.
Does that mean cancellation itself must always be prevented while a task has a borrow?

Not necessarily. The requirement is memory safety under cancellation, not a blanket prohibition on cancelling tasks that hold borrows. Whether a particular arrangement can be accepted depends on whether its resource remains valid throughout any possible use, including uses relevant to cancellation. The goal does not select a specific way of establishing that condition.
And how does task migration fit into the guarantee?

Migration means the checker cannot justify safety by assuming the task will remain in one execution context. A borrow that crosses into a task has to remain valid if that task migrates as well as if it does not. Migration does not by itself tell us that a particular program is safe or unsafe; it is another circumstance under which the ownership and borrowing guarantees must continue to hold.
I also want nested borrows represented in the programs. What is the core issue there?

With nested borrows, access can be derived through another borrow rather than directly from the resource’s owner. The important relationship is that derived access cannot remain usable after the access it depends on, or the underlying resource, has ceased to be valid. A task boundary can make that relationship less obvious, and cancellation can affect the task’s opportunity to use the derived access. The 12 safe and 12 unsafe programs need to cover nested borrows, but no particular allocation of programs among the requested topics is specified.
Could you give an abstract safe-versus-unsafe contrast without choosing language syntax?

At a high level, consider a resource and a task that has borrowed access to it. The safe side of the contrast is an arrangement in which the resource stays valid whenever that task might use the borrow, including with cancellation and migration. On the unsafe side, the resource could cease to be valid while the task could still use the borrow. A memory-safety guarantee requires the checker not to accept that unsafe arrangement. This is an illustration of the obligation, not one of the specified test programs.
What changes if ownership itself crosses a task boundary?

The checker then has to account for who may treat the resource as owned before and after the transfer, as well as any borrows that remain relevant. Transferring ownership must not make existing borrowed access dangle, and the former owner must not be treated as still having unrestricted ownership if that would conflict with the transfer. Those are general safety concerns; the goal does not commit to a particular ownership-transfer operation or implementation.
Is it possible for a program about ownership transfer to also exercise cancellation?

Yes, those are overlapping concerns rather than mutually exclusive categories. A program can involve an ownership transfer and a cancellation-sensitive period during which borrowed access matters. Likewise, a nested borrow can cross a task boundary. The coverage requirement names nested borrows, ownership transfer, and cancellation; it does not require the programs to fit into separate, nonoverlapping groups.
I want to be precise about the number of programs. Is it 12 in each category?

No. The stated target is 12 safe programs that the checker accepts and 12 unsafe programs that it rejects: 24 programs in total. Together they are to cover nested borrows, ownership transfer, and cancellation. There is no stated count for each category, nor a stated split of each category between the safe and unsafe sets.
Does accepting those 12 safe programs mean the checker must accept every possible memory-safe program?

That broader completeness claim is not part of the goal. It requires acceptance of the specified set of 12 safe programs and rejection of the specified set of 12 unsafe programs. The memory-safety guarantee is a separate, universal obligation for programs the checker accepts, including when cancellation and migration occur. Those requirements do not imply that every safe program must be accepted.
How should I understand the ban on whole-program analysis?

The guarantee cannot depend on inspecting the entire program as one unit to discover every way a task or resource might be used. The design therefore needs a way to establish its safety judgments without that global analysis. This is a constraint on the checker, not a statement that it may ignore interactions across task boundaries; those interactions are precisely what it must account for.
And no runtime borrow checks means the program cannot test at execution time whether a borrow is still valid?

The requested checker cannot rely on runtime borrow checks to enforce the borrowing guarantee. Its acceptance decision must provide the needed memory-safety assurance without deferring borrow validity to such checks during execution. That constraint is specifically about runtime borrow checks; it does not, by itself, describe or forbid ordinary runtime behavior involved in asynchronous tasks or cancellation.
Would it be enough to reason only about the moment a borrow crosses into a task?

No. The initial crossing matters, but the safety condition extends through every later point where the task could use that access. A borrow could be valid when handed over and invalid by the time it is used. Cancellation and migration must be included in that continuing reasoning rather than checked only at the transfer boundary.
So a check that works only when tasks finish normally would miss part of the goal?

Yes. The guarantee explicitly includes cancellation and task migration. Establishing safety solely for normal completion would leave those stated circumstances unaddressed. The same underlying question remains in each case: can a task access a borrowed resource at a time when that resource is no longer valid?
I do not want the discussion to confuse memory safety with whether cancellation behaves as an application expects.

They are different questions. Here, cancellation matters because it can affect the validity of borrowed access and thus memory safety. The goal does not specify application-level cancellation results, scheduling behavior, or progress guarantees. The checker’s required guarantee is that programs it accepts remain memory-safe under cancellation and migration.
How do nested borrows interact with that continuing validity requirement?

If a task can use access derived from another borrow, it is not enough to examine the derived access in isolation. Its continued use also depends on the validity of the access and resource beneath it. Cancellation or migration cannot make an otherwise invalid chain of access safe. Conversely, the mere presence of nesting is not itself a reason to call a program unsafe: the target includes safe programs covering nested borrows that the checker must accept.
Similarly, cancellation should not make every program unsafe just because a task holds a borrowed resource?

Correct. The requirement to accept 12 safe programs covering the requested topics rules out treating those topics as inherently disqualifying. The relevant distinction is whether borrowed access can remain valid through the circumstances the program permits. The checker must reject the 12 unsafe programs while still accepting the 12 safe ones; simply rejecting everything involving cancellation would not meet that target.
Could a checker satisfy the numerical test target by accepting the 12 safe programs but also accepting some unsafe program outside the set?

Not while satisfying the stated memory-safety guarantee. The 12 safe and 12 unsafe programs are an explicit acceptance-and-rejection target, but the guarantee is broader: accepted programs must be memory-safe under cancellation and task migration. The numerical target does not license accepting other programs that violate that guarantee.
What is the clearest way to state the design problem without implying we have already built or tested a checker?

State it as a goal: design an ownership type checker for cancellable asynchronous tasks that safely transfers borrowed resources across task boundaries; guarantee memory safety under cancellation and task migration without whole-program analysis or runtime borrow checks; and have it accept 12 safe programs and reject 12 unsafe programs covering nested borrows, ownership transfer, and cancellation. That describes the intended checker and its evaluation target, not a completed design or a reported test result.

For the ownership checker, I propose region-indexed task scopes, linear join obligations, cancellation-shielded child draining, and Send/Sync-qualified transfers for migration. How do those pieces fit together?

They address different parts of the same task-boundary problem. Region-indexed scopes would relate a child task’s borrowed access to a region in which that access must remain valid. Linear join obligations would account for outstanding children before their borrows can be treated as finished. Cancellation-shielded child draining would preserve that accounting when cancellation interrupts a parent’s normal path. Send/Sync-qualified transfers would constrain what may cross boundaries where a task can migrate. Together, these are a proposed design, not yet a demonstration that the safety goal has been met.
What does “region-indexed” add to a task scope?

It suggests that a scope carries a region relationship the checker can use when judging borrows transferred to tasks. The relevant question is whether the borrowed resource remains valid for as long as a child task could use it. Indexing the task scope by a region gives the proposed checker a way to express that relationship without making the borrow’s validity depend on an unrestricted, whole-program search. The proposal does not specify a particular notation for regions or a complete set of typing rules.
Does a region-indexed scope mean the child must finish before that region ends?

That is the intended safety relationship: a child must not retain usable borrowed access beyond the validity of the region on which that access depends. The other parts of the proposal are relevant because simply writing down a scope relationship is not enough if an outstanding child can outlive it, especially when cancellation changes the parent’s path. Exactly how the checker expresses and enforces the relationship remains to be designed.
Why introduce a linear join obligation rather than just saying that children should be joined?

A linear obligation makes the responsibility to account for an outstanding child something the ownership checker is meant to track, rather than a convention programmers may overlook. “Linear” suggests the obligation cannot simply be duplicated or silently discarded. Its role here is to prevent a parent from treating borrowed resources as free of a child’s potential uses while that child is still outstanding. This describes the rationale for the proposal; it does not establish a final rule for every possible join or transfer of an obligation.
Is a join obligation itself the borrowed resource?

No. The resource is what the task might access through a borrow. The proposed join obligation is an accounting responsibility associated with an outstanding task. The distinction matters: returning from a scope or cancelling a parent must not be mistaken for proof that the child can no longer use its borrow. The obligation is intended to keep that outstanding possibility visible to the checker.
What is meant by cancellation-shielded child draining?

It is a proposed way to handle outstanding child tasks when cancellation reaches the surrounding task. “Draining” suggests accounting for those children through completion or another appropriate end to their ability to use borrowed resources; “cancellation-shielded” suggests that this process is not itself cut short by the same cancellation. The point is to avoid leaving children with live borrowed access while the resources they depend on are allowed to cease being valid. The proposal does not yet define a concrete cancellation protocol.
Would shielding mean a child cannot be cancelled?

That does not follow from the proposal. The shielding is described in connection with child draining: it protects the process needed to account for outstanding children from being interrupted before the borrowing relationship is safe to end. It is not, by itself, a statement that children can never be cancelled or that cancellation is globally disabled.
Why isn't it sufficient to require joins on the normal return path?

Because the goal includes cancellation. A rule that accounts for children only when the parent follows its normal path leaves open what happens when that path is interrupted. Linear join obligations and cancellation-shielded child draining are proposed together so the responsibility for outstanding children is not lost just because cancellation occurs.
Does child draining count as a runtime borrow check, which the goal rules out?

They are different concepts. Draining concerns what happens to outstanding child tasks; a runtime borrow check would inspect or enforce borrow validity at execution time instead of relying on the type checker’s acceptance decision. The proposal uses draining to support the task-lifetime discipline while keeping borrow judgments in the proposed ownership checker. Whether a full design actually meets the no-runtime-borrow-check requirement would still need to be shown.
How do Send and Sync enter the picture?

They are qualifications on transfers relevant to migration. In their usual conceptual roles, Send concerns whether a value can be transferred across execution contexts, while Sync concerns whether shared access can be used safely across such contexts. Requiring Send/Sync qualifications where appropriate is intended to stop a borrow or owned value from crossing a task boundary in a way that becomes unsafe if the task migrates. The proposal does not spell out a complete rule for each kind of transfer.
Should I read “Send/Sync-qualified” as requiring both qualifications on every transfer?

No universal both-for-every-transfer rule is stated. The proposal names Send/Sync-qualified transfers for migration, but the applicable qualification depends on what is being transferred and how it may be accessed. A complete checker would need to make those distinctions explicit rather than treating the two terms as interchangeable.
If a transfer satisfies the relevant Send or Sync condition, is its borrow automatically safe?

No. Migration compatibility and borrow validity are separate questions. A transfer could be appropriately qualified for migration yet still be unsafe if a child can use a borrowed resource after the resource ceases to be valid. Conversely, accounting for the child’s lifetime does not alone settle whether migration permits the transfer. The proposed components are meant to work together, not substitute for one another.
How do these components relate to nested borrows?

A nested borrow adds a chain of access: a child’s usable access may depend on another borrow as well as on the underlying resource. Region-indexed task scopes could express the relevant validity relationships, while the join obligation and cancellation-shielded draining address whether a child could still use that access as the surrounding scope ends. Send/Sync qualifications remain relevant if the task or its access may migrate. This is an account of what the proposed components would have to handle, not a claim that all nested-borrow cases have been proved safe.
And for ownership transfer, which part is doing the work?

Ownership transfer raises questions about who retains authority over a resource and how outstanding borrows remain valid. The proposed ownership checker would need to relate that transfer to its region-indexed scopes and any linear join obligations for children that might still borrow the resource. Send/Sync qualifications address the separate migration aspect of a transfer. The proposal lists the components but does not specify a full ownership-transfer rule.
Could someone satisfy a join obligation while the child still has access to its borrow?

If that were permitted in a way that allowed the resource to become invalid while the child could still use it, it would undermine the intended safety argument. The proposal’s purpose is for accounting for a child to correspond to ending its relevant outstanding access. How that correspondence is formalized is an open design detail, rather than something already established by the phrase “linear join obligation.”
What happens to the obligation when the surrounding task is cancelled?

It must not simply disappear if a child can still use a borrowed resource. That is why the proposal pairs linear obligations with cancellation-shielded child draining: cancellation should not bypass the accounting needed before borrowed resources cease to be valid. The exact mechanics of discharging an obligation during cancellation are not specified here.
Would the shield itself prove memory safety under cancellation?

Not on its own. Shielding addresses interruption of child draining, but safety also depends on the region relationship actually keeping resources valid, on join obligations accurately representing outstanding access, and on transfers meeting the relevant migration constraints. A complete checker would need to show these pieces are coherent under cancellation and migration; naming the pieces is a design proposal, not that proof.
Does the proposal depend on whole-program analysis?

Its components suggest a more local discipline: scope indices express validity relationships, linear obligations track outstanding child responsibilities, and transfer qualifications constrain migration. That is consistent with the goal of avoiding whole-program analysis. But the proposal alone does not specify enough rules to demonstrate that every required judgment can be made without it.
Could the design simply reject every task that borrows a resource and still claim to use these components?

That would miss the purpose of safely transferring borrowed resources across task boundaries and would not satisfy the goal of accepting 12 safe programs covering nested borrows, ownership transfer, and cancellation. The proposed components are intended to distinguish permissible arrangements from unsafe ones, not to serve as labels for a blanket rejection of borrowing tasks.
And what should I avoid claiming about the 12 safe and 12 unsafe programs at this point?

Avoid saying the proposed checker has already accepted the 12 safe programs or rejected the 12 unsafe programs. Those are targets from the goal. The present proposal identifies mechanisms that might support the required distinctions, including the cases involving nested borrows, ownership transfer, and cancellation, but it contains no completed checker or reported test results.
Can you state the proposal in one precise sentence?

Use region-indexed task scopes to relate borrowed access to task lifetimes, linear join obligations to account for outstanding children, cancellation-shielded child draining to preserve that accounting during cancellation, and Send/Sync-qualified transfers to address task migration.
How can a cancelled parent keep a borrowed resource alive until every child using it has stopped?

The key is to separate cancellation of the parent’s normal work from the end of its responsibility for outstanding children. Under the proposed approach, the parent cannot let the relevant resource or borrow become invalid merely because cancellation has begun. Its linear join obligations still have to be accounted for, and cancellation-shielded child draining is intended to keep that process from being interrupted before the children can no longer use the resource. This is the safety relationship the design needs to establish, not yet a complete cancellation rule.
If the parent is cancelled, why doesn't its scope simply end at that point?

If ending the scope would invalidate a borrow that a child can still use, that would conflict with the memory-safety goal. The proposed region-indexed scope must therefore remain relevant until the outstanding child access it protects has ended. Cancellation can stop the parent’s ordinary course of work without making a still-running child’s borrow disappear.
What if the parent owns the resource rather than borrowing it?

Then the parent must not relinquish the resource while a child could still use its borrow. The proposed join obligations are meant to keep that outstanding use visible during cancellation. Only after the children that may use the resource have stopped can the parent treat their borrowed access as finished. The proposal does not specify the precise ownership or cleanup operations that would express this.
And if the parent is itself only borrowing the resource?

The parent cannot independently extend the underlying resource’s validity just by holding a borrow. The region relationship has to ensure that the resource remains valid through the children’s possible uses. If the parent passes borrowed access to a child, cancellation must not let the parent finish its part of that borrowing relationship while the child still relies on it. The proposed scope and join discipline would need to make that dependency enforceable.
So shielding is supposed to protect the resource from cancellation?

More precisely, the proposal shields child draining from being cut short by cancellation. That gives the parent a chance to account for outstanding child access before the protected borrow or resource becomes invalid. Shielding is not, by itself, a way to make an otherwise expired resource valid; the region and ownership relationships must support its continued validity too.
Could the parent just send a cancellation request to each child and then release the resource?

A request alone would not establish that the children have stopped using the resource. The required condition is about their possible access, not whether they have been asked to stop. If a child could still use its borrow after the resource is released, the arrangement is unsafe. The proposal calls for draining outstanding children rather than treating a cancellation request as proof that their access has ended.
Does draining mean the parent must wait for every child to finish normally?

The essential condition is that every relevant child has stopped being able to use the borrowed resource before its validity ends. The word “draining” indicates accounting for outstanding children through that point; it does not, on its own, require that each child finish by a normal-completion path. A full design would need to define what establishes that a child has stopped and how its join obligation is discharged.
Why do the join obligations have to be linear?

The linearity is intended to keep the responsibility for each outstanding child from being silently lost or treated as settled without accounting for that child. During cancellation, that matters because the parent’s normal path may be abandoned, but the child’s ability to use the resource may remain. Linearity alone does not keep the resource alive; it helps ensure the obligation to account for the child remains present.
If there are several children borrowing the same resource, can the parent release it after the first child stops?

Not if another child can still use it. The question’s condition is until every child using the resource has stopped. Each outstanding child that may rely on the resource has to be accounted for before the resource’s validity may end. The proposed obligations are meant to make that distinction explicit rather than treating one child’s completion as completion of the whole group.
What about a child that has already stopped before cancellation reaches the parent?

A child whose ability to use the borrow has already ended would not need to be kept running for the resource’s sake. What matters is whether any child remains able to use the resource when its validity might end. The proposed accounting must distinguish completed child access from outstanding child access; cancellation cannot be used to assume that an unaccounted-for child is finished.
Would the parent's borrow have to stay live for the entire draining period?

If a child’s access depends on the parent’s borrow, then the relevant borrowing relationship must remain valid while that child can use it. The proposed region-indexed scope is intended to express such dependencies, and draining is intended to prevent cancellation from ending them prematurely. The precise treatment of a parent’s borrow, including nested borrows, would need to be stated in the checker’s rules.
I'm worried that the parent might be cancelled again while it is draining. Wouldn't that interrupt the protection?

The proposed cancellation shield is meant to prevent cancellation from cutting off the child-draining responsibility before it is safe to end it. That includes the general concern that cancellation might otherwise interrupt the parent while children remain outstanding. The proposal does not define a particular model of repeated cancellation, so it would be premature to claim exactly how such an event is handled.
Is this saying cancellation cannot finish until the children have stopped?

For this proposed safety strategy, the parent cannot finish in a way that invalidates resources still borrowed by its children. That may require the parent’s cancellation path to continue accounting for children until their relevant access has ended. It is not a claim about every observable aspect of when cancellation is reported or completed; those details have not been specified.
Could this turn a memory-safety issue into a problem where cancellation takes a long time?

Yes, the two concerns are distinct. Keeping a resource valid until children have stopped addresses the safety condition, but it does not by itself guarantee how quickly they stop. The question here is how to avoid invalidating borrowed access under cancellation, not a specified bound on cancellation time or a progress guarantee.
Where does task migration matter while the parent is waiting for children?

Migration must not invalidate the borrow or make the transfer of access inappropriate for the execution context. The proposed Send/Sync qualifications address that aspect. They do not replace the need to keep the resource valid until the children have stopped, and the join and draining discipline does not replace migration qualifications. Both constraints must hold if a child may migrate.
Could the parent decide that a child has stopped merely because the parent's scope is being exited?

No. Scope exit cannot serve as proof of the very fact needed to make scope exit safe. If a child could still use the borrow, ending the protecting scope would risk invalidating its access. The proposed join obligations and child draining are meant to ensure that the parent accounts for outstanding children before allowing that end to take effect.
Does checking that a join obligation was discharged count as a runtime borrow check?

Not necessarily. A join obligation represents the responsibility to account for an outstanding child; a runtime borrow check would decide at execution time whether borrowed access is valid. In the proposed approach, the checker would have to ensure that its accepted programs preserve the obligation through cancellation, while the task-draining behavior ensures children have stopped before the relevant scope ends. The proposal has not yet supplied a complete account proving that this can be done without runtime borrow checks.
Can you put the answer in terms of what the parent must not assume?

It must not assume that its own cancellation stops its children, that a request for them to stop means they have stopped, or that exiting its ordinary control path ends their ability to use a borrow. Until every child that might use the resource is accounted for, the relevant resource and borrow relationships must remain valid. Region-indexed scopes, linear join obligations, and cancellation-shielded draining are the proposed means of maintaining that condition.

Here is a hypothesis about the cancelled-parent case: a linear join token, together with cancellation-safe scope cleanup that drains children before resource destruction, prevents dangling borrows after parent cancellation. Does that state the idea accurately?

Yes, as a hypothesis. The proposed order is crucial: cancellation does not allow the resource to be destroyed while children may still borrow it. The linear join token represents the outstanding responsibility for the children, and cancellation-safe scope cleanup drains them before resource destruction. If those relationships hold, the children should not be left with dangling borrows after the parent is cancelled. That is the proposed reasoning, not a demonstrated result.
What exactly is linear about the join token?

“Linear” means the token is meant to be accounted for rather than freely copied or silently discarded. In this hypothesis, its significance is that a cancelled parent cannot simply forget the responsibility associated with children that may still use a borrowed resource. The statement does not specify the token’s exact representation or the complete rules for using it.
Is the token supposed to keep the resource alive by itself?

Not by itself. The token represents an obligation; it is not the resource or a physical mechanism that extends its lifetime. The hypothesized protection depends on scope cleanup actually draining the children before resource destruction. The token matters because that responsibility must remain accounted for even when the parent is cancelled.
Why specify cancellation-safe scope cleanup instead of just ordinary cleanup?

Because the case at issue is parent cancellation. If cleanup could be abandoned by the cancellation it is meant to handle, children might remain able to use the borrowed resource when destruction occurs. Calling the scope cleanup cancellation-safe makes the proposed ordering apply to the cancellation path as well as to an ordinary path. The hypothesis does not specify a particular cleanup implementation.
What does it mean for that cleanup to drain children?

For this hypothesis, draining must account for children through the point where they can no longer use the borrowed resource. Merely initiating an attempt to stop them would not establish that point. The hypothesis places that draining before resource destruction, so the resource remains available during any outstanding child use.
Could cleanup destroy the resource as soon as it starts draining?

That would not preserve the order in the hypothesis. Cleanup must drain the children before resource destruction, not simply begin draining and destroy the resource while a child might still use its borrow. The proposed prevention of dangling borrows rests on that distinction.
Suppose the parent has already been cancelled. Why does the token still matter then?

Parent cancellation is precisely when the obligation must not disappear unnoticed. The hypothesis uses the linear join token to keep the outstanding child responsibility in view, while cancellation-safe scope cleanup carries out the draining before destruction. Cancelling the parent is not, by itself, evidence that the children have stopped borrowing the resource.
Am I claiming that the child tasks themselves are immune to cancellation?

No. The hypothesis says that scope cleanup is cancellation-safe and drains children before destroying the resource. It does not say children cannot be cancelled. The relevant condition is that no child remains able to use a borrow after the resource is destroyed, however its activity comes to an end.
Is joining a child the same thing as sending it a request to stop?

Not for the reasoning here. A request to stop leaves open whether the child can still use its borrow. The join-token and draining hypothesis depends on accounting for the child until that possible access has ended. Otherwise destroying the resource could still leave a dangling borrow.
What happens if there is more than one child borrowing the resource?

The ordering has to cover every child that could still use it. Draining one child would not justify destroying the resource if another child retained borrowed access. The hypothesis speaks of draining children before resource destruction; its safety rationale depends on that being sufficient for all relevant outstanding child uses.
Is resource destruction the same as parent cancellation?

No. The hypothesis specifically separates them. Parent cancellation may trigger the scope’s cleanup, but the resource is not to be destroyed until after the children have been drained. Treating cancellation itself as immediate permission to destroy the resource would erase the ordering on which the hypothesis relies.
What does “dangling borrow” mean in this statement?

It means borrowed access remains available after the resource it refers to has been destroyed. The hypothesis is that the token and cleanup ordering prevent that situation following parent cancellation: children finish their relevant access first, and resource destruction comes afterward.
Would a linear token alone be enough to support the conclusion?

No. A token could represent an outstanding responsibility, but if cleanup nevertheless destroyed the resource before the children stopped using it, the borrow could dangle. The hypothesis has two cooperating parts: a linear join token and cancellation-safe scope cleanup that drains children before resource destruction.
Would cancellation-safe cleanup alone be enough, without the token?

That would be a different hypothesis. Here, the linear join token is part of the proposed way to ensure that the responsibility for outstanding children remains accounted for, including when cancellation changes the parent’s path. The statement does not establish what alternative arrangements might or might not achieve the same result.
How careful should I be with the word “prevents” in the hypothesis?

Keep it conditional on the proposed mechanism doing what the statement requires. If the linear obligation cannot be lost, cleanup remains effective under parent cancellation, and children are drained before the resource is destroyed, then dangling borrows from those children should be prevented. The node presents that as a hypothesis; it does not report a proof, implementation, or test outcome.
Does the hypothesis tell us exactly when a join token is discharged?

No. It identifies a linear join token and the required ordering of draining and destruction, but it does not give a formal rule for discharging the token. Such a rule would have to respect the central condition: accounting for the token cannot justify resource destruction while a child may still use a borrow.
Could the resource be destroyed after the parent is cancelled but before cleanup finishes?

Not if cleanup has yet to drain children that may use it. The hypothesis explicitly places child draining before resource destruction. Cancellation may have happened already; what matters for avoiding a dangling borrow is that destruction waits until the relevant child access has stopped.
Is there an implied guarantee that draining always finishes quickly?

No. The hypothesis concerns the safety ordering after parent cancellation, not a bound on how long draining takes. Keeping a resource from being destroyed while children might still borrow it is a memory-safety condition; it does not itself establish prompt cancellation or completion.
Does this settle whether the proposed checker meets all its goals?

No. This is a hypothesis about one cancellation-related risk: dangling borrows after a parent is cancelled. It does not, on its own, demonstrate the full memory-safety guarantee, settle migration, or show acceptance of 12 safe programs and rejection of 12 unsafe programs. Its specific claim is the proposed connection between a linear join token, cancellation-safe draining before destruction, and the absence of dangling child borrows after parent cancellation.
Can you restate the hypothesis without making it sound like an observed result?

The hypothesis is that, if a linear join token preserves the obligation to account for borrowing children and cancellation-safe scope cleanup drains those children before destroying their borrowed resource, parent cancellation will not leave those children with dangling borrows.
I want to define cancellation-safe scope-exit lowering: cancel children, shield joins, then expire region loans. I also want to check nested borrows and migration. How should I read that plan?

Read it as an ordering for scope exit when children may still use borrowed resources. First, initiate cancellation of the children. Next, shield the joins so cancellation does not interrupt the process of accounting for those children. Only after that should the region loans expire. Checking nested borrows and migration is part of examining whether this proposed ordering handles the relevant access relationships; the plan is not yet a completed lowering or safety proof.
Why does cancelling the children come before joining them?

In this plan, cancellation asks the children to stop, while joining accounts for them through the point at which they have stopped. The two steps are not interchangeable: initiating cancellation alone does not establish that a child can no longer use a borrowed resource. The subsequent shielded joins are what prevent scope exit from moving straight to loan expiration while a child remains outstanding.
Does “cancel children” mean I can immediately expire their loans?

No. A cancellation request is not the same as the end of a child’s possible access. The plan explicitly puts shielded joins between cancelling children and expiring region loans. If a loan expired immediately after the cancellation request, a child might still be able to use the borrow it supports.
What exactly is being shielded in “shield joins”?

The joins are shielded from interruption by cancellation. That is meant to preserve the parent’s ability to account for its children before region loans expire. It does not mean the children are shielded from the cancellation requested in the preceding step.
Could I say that the joins finish the job that the cancellation request starts?

That captures the distinction at a high level. The cancellation step initiates stopping the children; the shielded joins are intended to ensure scope exit does not proceed as though they have stopped until they actually have. The plan has not specified the precise mechanics of either step, so it is better not to imply a particular child-cancellation protocol.
Why put region-loan expiration last?
